bib.title: Conditional Random Fields: Probabilistic Models for Segmenting and Labeling Sequence Data
bib.venue: ICML 2001 (venue not printed in the text; year and venue from the ledger request)

question: Can a discriminative sequence model with a single globally normalised exponential model avoid the label bias problem of MEMMs while keeping their ability to use arbitrary observation features?
hypothesis: CRFs solve label bias and are more robust than MEMMs and HMMs when the true data has higher-order dependencies than the model.
contributions: Introduce conditional random fields, a framework for segmenting and labeling sequences
Show the label bias problem of MEMMs and other per-state normalised models
Two iterative scaling algorithms (S and T) for parameter estimation, with a convergence sketch
Experiments on synthetic data and Penn treebank POS tagging comparing HMM, MEMM, CRF

method.summary: Chain-structured CRFs define p(y|x) as one exponential model normalised by Z(x) over whole label sequences, trained by maximum likelihood with improved iterative scaling variants using forward-backward. Compared with HMMs and MEMMs of identical state structure on synthetic HMM-generated data and POS tagging.
method.task: sequence labeling (POS tagging, synthetic label-bias and mixed-order tasks)

datasets.name: Label-bias synthetic (noisy rib/rob network)
datasets.source: generated from an HMM encoding Figure 1; each state emits its symbol with probability 29/32 and any other symbol with 1/32

datasets.name: Mixed-order synthetic HMMs
datasets.size: 1,000 sequences of length 25 per randomly generated model
datasets.split: sample used for training and testing (split not stated)
datasets.source: randomly chosen mixed first/second-order HMMs, 5 labels a-e, 26 observation values A-Z, sparse tables (at most 2 or 3 nonzero entries)

models.name: CRF
models.architecture: chain CRF with features f_k on edges and g_k on vertices
models.init_from: all-zero parameters; CRF+ initialised from converged MEMM+ parameters

models.name: MEMM
models.architecture: per-state exponential models over next states

training.objective: maximise conditional log-likelihood O(theta)=sum_i log p_theta(y_i|x_i)
training.optimizer: improved iterative scaling: Algorithm S (slack feature) and Algorithm T (per-T(x) counters, Newton roots)
training.steps: synthetic mixed-order: CRF about 500 iterations, MEMM about 100; POS: MEMM+ about 100 iterations, CRF+ 1,000 iterations (from MEMM init), CRF from uniform not converged after 2,000
training.compute: about 0.2 seconds per CRF iteration (mixed-order synthetic)

other.convergence: stopped at stabilisation / convergence of iterative scaling; criterion not given
other.POS features: tag-word mu_{y,x} and tag-tag lambda_{y',y}; spelling features: begins with number or upper case, contains hyphen, suffixes -ing -ogy -ed -s -ly -ion -tion -ity -ies

inference.decoding: Viterbi (forward-backward decoding gave no significant change)
inference.samples: synthetic: several runs, one error rate per test set; POS: one run per model

metrics.name: error rate
metrics.definition: synthetic: test-set label error; POS: per-word error

metrics.name: oov error
metrics.definition: per-word error on out-of-vocabulary words not seen in training

eval.protocol: single runs; no significance tests, seeds or confidence intervals stated

results.setup: Noisy rib/rob HMM data, 2,000 train and 500 test samples, same topology, identity-of-symbol features, typical run
results.quote: the CRF error is 4.6% while the MEMM error is 42%,

results.table: Fig 4 table, row CRF, column error

results.table: Fig 4 table, row CRF, column oov error

results.claim: Spelling features cut overall error by around 25% for MEMM and CRF.
results.setup: Same POS setup, MEMM and CRF with orthographic features

results.claim: On mixed-order synthetic data the CRF usually beats the MEMM by 10%-20% relative error.
results.setup: Random mixed first/second-order HMMs, 5 labels, 26 observations, 1,000 sequences of length 25; first-order models trained; points with alpha<0.01 are exceptions
results.quote: often by a wide margin of 10%–20%

results.claim: CRF training from uniform start had not converged after 2,000 iterations, while CRF+ initialised from MEMM+ converged in 1,000.
CRF training on synthetic data takes about 500 iterations versus about 100 for the MEMM.
MEMMs earlier reported as doubling precision relative to HMMs on a FAQ segmentation task.
results.setup: FAQ segmentation task, MEMMs vs HMMs, as reported by McCallum et al. 2000

limits: Main stated limitation: slow convergence of training relative to MEMMs and HMMs.
Convergence proof is only sketched; full proof deferred.
No learning rate, regularisation, seeds or significance tests; single runs on POS; no held-out dev set.
Synthetic experiments do not test the extra representational power of CRFs over HMMs (Fig 3 caption).
Without spelling features the HMM beats the CRF on oov error (45.99% vs 48.05%).
Only chain-structured CRFs and a first-order model are tested; tree-structured CRFs, feature induction and boosting-style training left to future work.
Iterative scaling has been superseded by gradient methods such as L-BFGS (from general knowledge, not stated in the paper).
